did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with difficult news: Isaiah tells Hezekiah to put his house in order because he is destined to die and will not recover.
In response to Isaiah’s words, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays to the Lord; the description emphasizes his personal and direct appeal to God.
In his prayer, Hezekiah recalls his faithfulness: he asks the Lord to remember that he walked before Him faithfully, with a whole heart, and did what was good in His sight.
The Lord answers Hezekiah’s prayer and adds fifteen years to his life. In addition, He promises to save him and Jerusalem from the king of Assyria.
The sign given to Hezekiah is extraordinary: the shadow on Ahaz’s stairway moves backward ten steps as a sign of the Lord’s word.
The chapter includes a letter or song by Hezekiah after his illness and recovery; from this point onward, he describes in the first person his fear of death and his hope for life.
Hezekiah describes his illness as cutting his life short midway through the journey, and his descent to the gates of Sheol as an image of approaching death.
In describing his suffering, Hezekiah uses images of a chirping bird and a mourning dove, and asks the Lord to intervene and be his advocate.
Hezekiah emphasizes the difference between the dead and the living: Sheol and death do not praise the Lord, whereas the living can praise Him and tell future generations of His faithfulness.
Isaiah commands that a cake of figs be applied to Hezekiah’s boil, and the chapter ends with Hezekiah asking for a sign that will enable him to go up to the house of the Lord.
